entries.n: Generally but not always used of death by a judicial sentence.
The same Hebrew word is elsewhere rendered 'allowance'.
The weak form 'digged' is used throughout in preference to 'dug', as contemporary writers did.
The prefix 'dis-' here is intensive, not negative; a stronger form of 'annul'.
Formerly by any of the senses, not restricted to sight as at present.
Literally to unfasten, then to break up a mass into its parts.
From a negative 'dis-' and 'cover'; 'discovereth the forests' means strips off their leaves.

entries.m: the act or office of weighing out or distributing, as a steward does
entries.n: From Latin 'to weigh'; the Greek word is the source of 'economy'.
The translators followed the Rheims version.
'Resolve' is used in the same sense in Shakespeare.

entries.m: the staff on which flax was rolled in spinning
entries.n: From Old English. The Hebrew conveys the idea of roundness; the instrument is obsolete.

entries.m: one who predicts future events by divination
entries.n: From Latin 'to foretell'; naturalized by a Saxon ending.
